title: Kateri Tekakwitha (1656–1680)
hookLine: a Mohawk and Algonquin woman, scarred by smallpox, later named a saint

cards: A girl in a Mohawk village keeps a blanket pulled over her head when she goes outside. Smallpox swept through when she was small. It took her parents, marked her face and weakened her eyes, so bright light hurts.
Her mother had been an Algonquin Christian; her father was Mohawk. She grows up in her uncle's longhouse, quiet, skilled with her hands, and saying no to the marriage her family wants for her.
Then black-robed priests come to the village. Today, Kateri Tekakwitha.

teach.b: First, two peoples in one person. Kateri carried both, Mohawk and Algonquin.
Catholics remember her as a saint of Indigenous North America, and some Indigenous Catholics speak of her as one of their own, not as someone the missionaries made. Second, baptism.
She asked a Jesuit, Jacques de Lamberville, to teach her, and he baptized her.

She took the name Catherine; Kateri is the Mohawk way of saying it. Some in her village turned on her. The early accounts tell of mockery and threats, some of it because she refused to work on Sundays.
She left, on foot and by canoe, for a Christian mission village near Montreal, where Mohawk and other Native Christians lived together.
There she prayed long hours, cared for the sick and old, and promised God never to marry. Her penances were severe, and she was never strong. She died young.
The Jesuits who knew her wrote her life, and one recorded that after she died, the scars on her face faded. Catholics hand it down as his testimony, an eyewitness's word.
The Church named her Venerable, then Blessed, then a saint.
People call her the Lily of the Mohawks, and some Catholics hear in that name a line from the Song of Songs, in the Douay-Rheims: "As the lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters."
A lily, growing where no one expected it.

how: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Kateri Tekakwitha, and her shrines in New York and Quebec draw pilgrims; Indigenous Catholic gatherings in North America often bear her name.

games.q: you're Kateri. you've been baptized, and some in your village mock and threaten you. what do you do?
o: give up the faith to keep the peace.

leave for a Christian mission village near Montreal.
games.why: she made the journey on foot and by canoe, and lived the rest of her short life there in prayer and care for the sick.

practice: Across the Americas, Native communities keep the faith in their own languages, songs and memories, some of them painful; let one come to mind, a nation whose land you live on or a name you've heard.
If you pray, ask Kateri Tekakwitha to pray for them; if not, hold them with respect. And if this week's stories have been heavy, let yourself rest here.

wordCard.voice: Kateri Tekakwitha. A Mohawk and Algonquin woman, scarred by smallpox, baptized against her village's wishes, who walked to a mission and gave her life to prayer and the sick.

carryVoice: Your line: lily of the mohawks. The week ran from hidden priests and Galileo to Ricci in China, then Lima, Cartagena and the northern forests. A week, complete.
